blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Discount is always calculated on the Marked Price (MP) to arrive at the final Selling Price (SP).
Successive discounts apply consecutive percentage reductions sequentially on the reduced price.
A Single Equivalent Discount combines multiple successive discount percentages into one effective overall discount rate.
Profit after discount depends directly on the relationship between Cost Price (CP), Marked Price (MP), and Selling Price (SP).

blocks.content: Cost Price (CP): Price at which the shopkeeper purchases the article. Marked Price (MP): The labelled price on the article (also called List Price). Discount: Reduction offered on the marked price to attract customers.
Selling Price (SP): Final price paid by the customer. Relationship: SP = MP − Discount
Discount % = (Discount / MP) × 100 SP = MP × (100 − Discount%) / 100 MP = SP × 100 / (100 − Discount%) When discount is d%:

An article is marked at ₹2000 and is sold after allowing a discount of 25%. We are required to find the selling price.
Step 1: Recall that discount is always calculated on the marked price. Therefore, we first calculate 25% of ₹2000.
Step 2: Subtract the discount from the marked price to obtain the selling price. Selling Price = 2000 − 500 = ₹1500.
Final Answer: The selling price of the article is ₹1500.

blocks.content: A trader marks his goods 40% above the cost price and then allows a discount of 20%. We are required to find the profit percentage.
Step 1: Assume the cost price is ₹100 to simplify percentage calculations. Step 2: Since the goods are marked 40% above cost price:
Marked Price = 100 + 40 = ₹140. Step 3: Calculate the discount.
Discount = 20% of 140 = ₹28. Step 4: Determine the selling price. Selling Price = 140 − 28 = ₹112.
Step 6: Convert profit into percentage. Profit % = (12/100) × 100 = 12%.
Final Answer: The trader earns a profit of 12%.
A shopkeeper allows a discount of 10% on the marked price and still makes a profit of 20%. We need to find the markup percentage.
Step 1: Assume the cost price is ₹100.
Step 2: A profit of 20% means the selling price becomes ₹120.
Step 3: After a discount of 10%, the customer pays 90% of the marked price. Therefore: 0.9 × MP = 120
Step 4: Solve for the marked price. MP = 120 ÷ 0.9 = ₹133.33 (approx.)
Final Answer: The markup is approximately 33.33%.

items: Questions on calculating single equivalent discount for two or more successive discounts are extremely high-frequency in RRB and competitive exams.
Markup percentage vs Discount percentage relationships frequently form the core of moderate-to-hard level profit and loss problems.
Always remember: Discount % = (Discount / Marked Price) × 100, whereas Profit % = (Profit / Cost Price) × 100.
